newsitem.title: CUBA: U.S.-blacklisted Sherritt to hold meeting in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-blacklisted Sherritt to hold meeting in Cuba.

text.p: Directors of Canada's Sherritt International Corp, one of the main foreign investors in Cuba targeted by U.S. sanctions, will hold a board meeting on the island Friday, a senior company executive said Wednesday.

Patrice Merrin Best, Sherritt's vice president for corporate affairs, told Reuters that the meeting in Havana would involve seven of the directors and officers who were barred from entering to the United States in July.
"All of the directors will be present and accounted for," said Merrin Best, speaking by telephone from Toronto.
It will mark the first time Sherritt has held a board meeting in Cuba, where the company has investments in nickel mining, oil exploration, tourism and agriculture.
The Havana meeting is a further sign that Sherritt is determined to withstand strong pressure from the U.S. government for the company to disinvest from Cuba.

In addition to Sherritt Chairman Ian Delaney, the meeting would include two prominent British businessmen -- Rupert Pennant-Rea, former deputy governor of the Bank of England, and Sir Patrick Sheehy, a former B.A.T Industries Plc chairman. Both men are on the Sherritt board.

Those Canadian and British executives were banned from entering the United States under Title IV of the so-called Helms-Burton law, enacted in March. Sherritt was the first foreign company in Cuba to be targeted by its provisions.

The U.S. law seeks to tighten the longstanding U.S. economic embargo against Communist-ruled Cuba by penalizing foreign companies and their executives who "traffic" in expropriated properties and assets in Cuba formerly owned by U.S. nationals or Cubans who later took U.S. citizenship.
Merrin Best described the Havana board meeting as "routine" but said she was aware that the U.S. authorities might view it as further evidence of the company's business links with Cuba.
During the session, the board is scheduled to review the company's Cuban operations, hear auditors' reports and discuss the overall business environment.
Sherritt's Delaney has said in the past the company has considered expanding its business in Cuba to include transportation, communications and financial projects.
Sherritt's investments in Cuba, estimated at more than $200 million, have made the company one of the most prominent investors on the island.

Sherritt's joint venture in the Cuban nickel industry faces claims from former U.S. owners of a nickel plant and nickel ore reserves who operated on the island before the nationalizations that followed the 1959 revolution.
U.S. allies such as Canada and Britain fiercely oppose the Helms-Burton law and have strongly protested the ban on Sherritt executives entering the United States.
U.S. authorities have also barred entry by executives of Grupo Domos, a Mexican telecommunications concern with a telephone joint venture in Cuba.
